investment_scope.basis: Generalist, and the base says so unusually clearly: no single sector reaches 18% of the book. Recomputed off the grind's own focus column over all 596 rows — Data Infrastructure 106, Healthcare & Bio 82, Industrial & Robotics 72, Consumer & Marketplaces 72, SaaS 54, Security 53, Fintech & Payments 50, Media/Gaming/Advertising 50, AI & Applied AI 26, DevTools & APIs 23, with Crypto & Web3 and Climate & Energy at 4 each and below the publication floor. The shape is a fifty-year book read at once: the networking, storage and semiconductor heritage still outweighs the AI wave the firm is now all-in on, because focus records what a company DOES and not when it was bought.

history.value: Menlo Ventures was founded on Sand Hill Road in 1976 by H. DuBose Montgomery, a 27-year-old electrical engineer out of Bell Labs, and is the oldest firm in this project's book. Its first two decades ran through the hardware and networking build-out — Dysan, Eldec, Valid Logic, LSI Logic and Sanmina in the late 1970s and 1980s, then StrataCom, Kalpana, SynOptics and Chipcom, four Ethernet and ATM companies Cisco, Nortel and 3Com bought between 1994 and 1996 — alongside a healthcare practice that backed Gilead Sciences in 1988 and Pyxis, IVAC and VNUS Medical. The internet era brought Hotmail, Infoseek, UUNET, F5 and Digital Insight. A 2010s consumer and enterprise book followed: Menlo led Uber's $32M Series B in 2011, backed Siri before Apple bought it, and led or joined Roku, Tumblr, Warby Parker, Dropcam, Poshmark, Betterment, eero, PillPack, Carta, Chime, Benchling and Recursion. In 2023 the firm made its first investment in Anthropic when the company was pre-product, led its $750M Series D a year later — the largest cheque in its history — and launched the $100M Anthology Fund with Anthropic in July 2024. It marked its fiftieth anniversary in June 2026 by announcing $3 billion of new capital across Menlo Ventures XVII and Menlo Inflection IV.
history.basis: The firm's own 50th-anniversary post supplies the founding, the Anthropic sequence and the $3B raise; every company named is a member row in the landed base, and the 1970s-1990s names come from the firm's own archived sector and Prior Investments pages (1998-2007).

investment_concept.value: Two funds, one ladder. Menlo Ventures XVII writes seed and Series A cheques into companies that may still be a small technical team, and Menlo Inflection IV provides growth capital from Series B onward into the same names as they break out — the firm's stated intent is to meet founders early and scale with them in every round that follows, which its own portfolio milestones bear out: of the 214 companies whose entry round the firm publishes, 36% entered at Series A, 29% at Series B, 15% at seed and 13% at Series C. Dedicated single-company vehicles carry the largest positions (two $500M funds for Anthropic alone), and the Anthology Fund, a $100M partnership with Anthropic, writes pre-seed and seed cheques from $100,000 up into AI-native teams, more than sixty of them so far.
investment_concept.basis: The two-fund ladder is the firm's own framing. The entry-round percentages are computed from the 214 portfolio cards that carry a Milestones entry — the class-1 layer this run's calibration gate scored at 33/34 — and not from the firm's prose.
